part_title: Amazon EMR: Distributed Processing, Usage Patterns and Frameworks

scenes.title: Amazon EMR overview
scenes.narration: The diagram starts with data in S3, such as logs, clickstreams and CSV records, then shows an Amazon EMR cluster processing it into curated outputs in S3. Look at the three node roles. A master or primary node coordinates work and manages the cluster. Core nodes provide distributed processing and, for some configurations, HDFS storage. Task nodes add processing capacity without holding HDFS data, making them useful for appropriate elastic jobs. Apache Spark is shown as a processing framework that divides a large transformation into work spread across nodes. The output includes cleaned data, aggregates and feature sets suitable for analytics or machine learning. A key architectural distinction is that input and durable output can live in S3 independently of the cluster lifecycle, so the cluster needn't be the permanent system of record. Scaling workers and selecting Spot capacity can reduce costs for suitable fault-tolerant tasks, but availability and job retry behavior matter. EMR manages the execution platform; you still decide the processing logic, data format, permissions and cluster sizing.

scenes.title: EMR usage patterns
scenes.narration: This slide compares three ways to run EMR, and each one fits a different workload. The left-hand transient batch cluster starts for a defined ETL or analytics job, reads data, writes results to S3 and terminates. That avoids paying for idle cluster instances between periodic runs. The middle long-running cluster stays available for interactive exploration or steady processing, potentially supporting several users and repeated workloads. Its economics depend on how much of its capacity remains busy. On the right, EMR Serverless runs supported applications without asking your team to provision or terminate a cluster manually. It provisions and scales resources based on workload demand. Trace the common input and output paths: S3 can hold persistent data for each pattern even though the compute model differs. A transient cluster is not automatically cheaper if startup overhead dominates many tiny jobs; similarly a persistent cluster wastes money when mostly idle. Choose by job duration, interactivity, predictability, framework support, operational overhead and security requirements rather than just the product label.

scenes.title: EMR frameworks and applications
scenes.narration: This slide explains why EMR supports multiple distributed frameworks on a common data-processing platform. Apache Spark provides distributed DataFrames, Spark SQL, batch processing and selected streaming or machine-learning workloads. Hive exposes SQL-style analysis and metastore-oriented data organisation. Presto or Trino is often selected for interactive distributed SQL over compatible sources. Look at the shared-data panel: teams can work on datasets in S3 or other supported storage while choosing an execution engine that suits each task. A data engineer might run a Spark transformation to curate model-evaluation logs, while an analyst uses an interactive SQL engine to inspect the prepared output. The underlying primary, core and task nodes support scheduling and execution in a cluster-based configuration. Framework selection doesn't waive the need for correct IAM roles, network paths or S3 access. It also doesn't mean every query engine offers identical performance or semantics. Match the operation—heavy ETL, ongoing distributed processing or low-latency interactive SQL—to the appropriate framework and cluster usage pattern.
